title: Motivations for pro-wildlife gardening: the role of nature connectedness
content:
Abstract
Residential gardens can contribute substantially to urban greenspace to support biodiversity and can be one of the main sources of contact with nature for urban residents. To meet these goals, garden managers need to be willing and able to include wildlife-friendly features in their garden. We used a self-reporting questionnaire distributed to residents of Derby, UK, to understand the drivers or indicators of wildlife-friendly gardening. In particular, we asked what motivates people to garden for wildlife, whether people are willing to change behaviours in their garden and neighbourhood, and how these behaviours relate to sociodemographic variables and nature connectedness. Of the 255 responses received, all had some outdoor space available to them, and almost all had private gardens. Motivations for gardening were split into how people used their gardens, either as outdoor spaces that included nature, or as social spaces. Respondents were prepared to see more dramatic changes to their neighbourhoods than their gardens that would support biodiversity, but willingness to change was generally limited. Respondents’ nature connectedness scores were related to gardening use and motivations, but we did not detect relationships with other sociodemographic variables. Our findings suggest that to engage residential garden managers in wildlife-friendly gardening, understanding how people use their gardens, and their existing nature connectedness is important. Also, pro-wildlife changes to public space are likely to be more popular than to private spaces. Further exploration of the relationship between nature connectedness and conservation behaviours could help to understand how to support wildlife-friendly gardening.
